newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Canberra cuts defence bureaucracy, boosts weapons.
newsitem.headline: Canberra cuts defence bureaucracy, boosts weapons.

text.p: Australia, strapped for cash but feeling its strategic superiority in Southeast Asia slipping away, on Friday announced a sweeping attack on defence bureaucracy aimed at boosting its frontline operations.
"We're going to shift expenditure from the bureaucracy of defence into the front line of defence," Prime Minister John Howard said.
"There'll be more money to spend on equipment and on the sharp end, the front end. So, it's fewer bureaucrats and more soldiers," Howard said.
Defence Minister Ian McLachlan on Friday said 8,000 defence support jobs would go under a defence review, with many uniformed staff redeployed to combat positions.
The reforms should ultimately shift up to A$1.0 billion (US$780 million) of the A$10 billion-a-year defence budget away from administration and into weapons and training, he said.

The Australian Defence Force has about 57,000 active personnel and some 49,000 reserves. About A$6 billion of the A$10 billion defence budget goes to the Navy, Army and Air Force, with the remainder spent on administration.
U.S. and European aerospace companies are competing to equip the Australian air force with up to A$660 million worth of missiles to hit targets from long range.

The air force plans to equip its 36 F-111 strike bombers with three types of stand-off missiles: a standard model to hit ordinary ground targets such as bridges, a specialist one that homes in on radars and third designed to pierce thick concrete.

Defence officials told Reuters that a small number had been ordered for training and the next step was to order a so-called war stock -- something like a hundred or more -- and have the missile operational by July 1998.
McLachlan said Australia's inefficient defence bureaucracy had to be squeezed in order to bolster falling defence spending in a post Cold War world where regional instability had risen.
"Post-Cold War, things are less certain than they were," he said, noting that defence spending had fallen from 2.6 percent of gross domestic product 10 years ago to 1.8 percent now.

Author of the defence review, Malcolm McIntosh, a former British defence procurement chief, said Australia needed to strengthen its defence front line as economically booming Asian nations boosted their military strength.
"Not that long ago, we were a mini-superpower in our own region," McIntosh told reporters on Friday.
"Our economy was substantially larger and the amount we bought for our defence dollar was substantially larger than anyone else around our region.

"That's changing and changing very quickly...the economies around the region are growing rapidly and all of those countries are now in a position to acquire the sort of things that only we could afford a few years ago," he said.
Although Australia's armed forces are still the most powerful south of China and east of India, its neighbours now operate the advanced equipment it once monopolised.
Since World War Two and until the 1980s Australia was alone in the region with its leading-edge fighter aircraft.
Even now, its 70-odd F/A-18 Hornets are an up-to-date fighter force, but Malaysia also operates Hornets and Indonesia has a handful of the similarly modern F-16.
McLachlan said Australia had no regional enemies but felt it had to respond to other countries' capabilities rather than their intentions -- which could change quickly.
